references.text: The immediate context: Jesus tells the parable about calculating the costs before building a tower. [ref:Luk 14:28-29|Luke 14:28-29] describes the man who sits down to calculate the expenses but does not have enough to finish – verse 30 is the mocking conclusion from the onlookers.

[ref:Ordsp 24:27|Proverbs 24:27] emphasizes the importance of finishing preparations before starting to build: "Do your work outside first and get it ready in the field, then build your house." The same principle of planning before building.

[ref:Jos 9:14-15|Joshua 9:14-15] shows an example of acting without consulting the Lord first – the Gibeonites deceived Israel because they did not seek God's counsel. The parallel is the danger of acting without careful consideration.

[ref:1 Kong 6:1-38|1 Kings 6:1-38] tells about Solomon's temple construction, which was completed after careful planning and calculation. Solomon is a positive counterpart to the man in the parable who could not complete his building project.

[ref:Luk 9:62|Luke 9:62] deals with the one who puts his hand on the plow and looks back, and who is not fit for God's kingdom. The same theme of starting something without finishing it, in connection with discipleship.

The point of the parable is summarized in [ref:Luk 14:33|Luke 14:33]: "So therefore none of you can be my disciple unless he gives up all that he has." The mockery over the unfinished building illustrates the cost of half-hearted discipleship.

[ref:Fil 1:6|Philippians 1:6] provides the theological counterweight: "He who began a good work in you will bring it to completion." In contrast to the man who could not finish, God completes what He begins.

[ref:Hebr 12:1-2|Hebrews 12:1-2] encourages running with endurance and looking to Jesus, the founder and perfecter of faith. The theme of finishing what one has started is central, in contrast to the man's inability to complete in Luke 14:30.

[ref:2 Kor 8:10-11|2 Corinthians 8:10-11] encourages completing what one has begun: "Now finish the work also, so that your completion may match your eagerness." A direct parallel to the theme of starting something without being able to complete it.
